newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Peru deal ends Latin debt crisis-Rhodes.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Peru deal ends Latin debt crisis-Rhodes.

text.p: Peru's completion of its external-debt financing plan with its commercial bank creditors has put an end to the Latin American debt crisis, said William Rhodes, Vice Chairman of Citibank.

"What we are seeing here is really the end of the Latin American debt crisis because this is the last major country that had an outstanding problem. Of the major countries, this is it. Peru was the last outstanding one," Rhodes told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"It's taken 14 years, but this is finally settled, closed and done," Rhodes said.

Rhodes said Peru had three problems over the years. "They had to settle with the Paris Club, they had to settle with Russia, and they had the commercial banks and now this was the last leg of the arrangement."
Rhodes said the completion of the deal will now allow Peru access to the international capital markets.
"I think what this will do is that it will allow Peru access to the international markets if they choose to do an international issue."
However, Rhodes said he did not know when or if Peru planned to tap the international markets.
Peru's external-debt financing plan covered an original principal amount of $4.3 billion in medium- and long-term commercial debt.

Under the Brady plan, the Peruvian government issued $560 million in discount bonds, $182 million in par bonds, $1.7 billion in front-loaded interest reduction bonds and $2.4 billion in past-due interest bonds.
The government also repurchased $2.6 billion of principal and past-due interest of eligible debt under a debt buyback.
Citibank was chair of the Bank Advisory Committee.

Asked whether there would be a continuance of new issuance out of Latin America going forward, Rhodes said: "I think what you are looking at is a highly liquid market internationally and so I think a lot of people are looking at Latin America because the economic reforms are moving ahead."

"Also there is some yield chasing going on but I think people feel that the countries are continuing to move on the economic reform road and there has been a major recovery since the Mexico problem in 1994-95, so there is a lot more confidence."
Rhodes also said there was likely to be more refinancings in the market of Brady bonds because of the high liquidity and lower yield spreads. "I think you will see more of those going forward."
